subject: Help with (Un)pooled regression´s and model comparisons

messages.author: 3ba9c13174149f8d
messages.subject: Help with (Un)pooled regression´s and model comparisons
parts:
Hello everybody,

Sorry already for that long posting. I just thougth better provide to much than less data and information for you ;)

I am now sitting here try to figure out how to run my analyses correctly telling me what I want. I did read already some former threads and catch up some further things resulting in further questions. Just starting at the beginning...
I have a 3D landmark data set from nine different species including males and females. The species differ in a reproductive trait. My main aim is to figure out whether the pattern of sexual dimorphism (SD) is different across (some) species and reproductive trait, respectively.

First, I just thought to split my dataset per species and analyse them all separately, visualize SD and see what are common and uncommon shape changes between species. But now I think this would not be the best way to do so. In an GeometricMorphometrics-course I learned about unpooled and pooled regressions to find relationships between shape and a variable (in my case "sex") either between groups or in all groups (= "species" in my case). If I remember it right, a pooled regression shows me the common aspects of SD in all species, while an unpooled regression should somehow reveal patterns of SD differnt in species?! Actually, I do not find often these terms "un-pooled regression" here, making it a bit hard for me to pick out the right things for my question.
What I read here, I concluded that I should achive this by running different models in procD.lm and apply a model comparison to figure out which factors explain shape variation in my data. I tried now to go step by step increasing the models by the differnet factors.

I started first with centroid size (CS).

gdf<-geomorph.data.frame(shape=coords,CS=CS_hum,sex=sexH,species=speciesH)
allo<-procD.lm(shape~CS,data=gdf,iter=9999,RRPP=F,print.progress=F)
anova(allo)

Showing me that CS has an effect and that allometry is present in my shape data.

Next I looked at whether species show different allometric trajectories:

##common allometry between species#
commonAllo<-procD.lm(shape~CS+species,data=gdf,iter=9999,RRPP=F,print.progress=F)

##unique allometry between species#
uniqueAllo<-procD.lm(shape~CS*species,data=gdf,iter=9999,RRPP=F,print.progress=F)

anova(commonAllo,uniqueAllo,print.progress=F)

As the unique allometry model is significant, it tells me that species exhibit different allometric trajectories, which is also obvious form the graph.

plotAllometry(uniqueAllo,size=CS,logsz=T,method="PredLine",pch=symbolsH,col=colourH)


I did the same thing for "sex" only.

commonAlloSex<-procD.lm(shape~CS+sex,data=gdf,iter=9999,RRPP=F,print.progress=F)
uniqueAlloSex<-procD.lm(shape~CS*sex,data=gdf,iter=9999,RRPP=F,print.progress=F)
anova(commonAlloSex,uniqueAlloSex)


                                      ResDf Df    RSS       SS       MS       Rsq      F        Z      P Pr(>F)

shape ~ CS * sex            222  1 1.4527 0.004203 0.004203 0.0026325 0.6423 -0.62949 0.7346      
Total                               225    1.5966                                                         

plotAllometry(commonAlloSex,size=CS,logsz=T,method="PredLine",pch=sexsymbols,col=colourH) #males=triangles


Here, I do not have a significant interaction CS:sex, thus no different allometries in males and females.

Combining now sex and species I am a bit uncertain how to do that correctly. First, I realized that connecting to variables with "*" and "/" are different things, "/" assigning a variable to a random effect. So far, I am not sure whether "species" should be a random effect in my case?

If I understod right, I could simply test for "sex"-effect with the following code (ignoring CS for the moment):

null_sex<-procD.lm(shape~species,data=gdf,iter=9999,RRPP=F,print.progress=F)
full_sex<-procD.lm(shape~species+sex,data=gdf,iter=9999,RRPP=F,print.progress=F)
anova(null_sex,full_sex)

                                     ResDf Df    RSS       SS       MS      Rsq      F      Z     P Pr(>F)
shape ~ species (Null)     217  1 1.0538                             0.000000                          
shape ~ species + sex    216  1 1.0101 0.043746 0.043746 0.027399 9.3547 5.3375 1e-04      
Total                              225    1.5966                                                     


...and otherwise for the "species"-effect with that one including pairwise comparison to check which species are different to each other:

null_species<-procD.lm(shape~sex,data=gdf,iter=9999,RRPP=F,print.progress=F)
full_species<-procD.lm(shape~sex+species,data=gdf,iter=9999,RRPP=F,print.progress=F)
anova(null_species,full_species)

                                     ResDf Df    RSS      SS      MS     Rsq      F      Z     P Pr(>F)
shape ~ sex (Null)          224  1 1.5219                         0.00000                          
shape ~ sex + species   216  8 1.0101 0.51184 0.06398 0.32058 13.682 13.477 1e-04      
Total                             225    1.5966                                                  

pw_species<-pairwise(full_species,groups=speciesH)
summary(pw_species,confidence=0.95,test.type="dist")

As allometry differ between species it should be of course included in the model. Or would it be possible/make sense to create first allometry-free shapes and then apply those to the models?
Further, I test with those only whether sex or species explains a significant amount of shape variation and not whether different sex-differences occur between species.

A model with the interaction of sex:species reveals it as not significant.

model<-procD.lm(shape~sex*species,data=gdf,iter=9999,RRPP=F,print.progress=F)
anova(model)

                    Df      SS       MS     Rsq       F       Z Pr(>F)   
species         8 0.54278 0.067847 0.33996 14.6551 13.3540  1e-04 ***
sex               1 0.04375 0.043746 0.02740  9.4492  4.6527    1e-04 ***
species:sex   8 0.04713 0.005892 0.02952  1.2726  1.3046    0.0988 . 
Residuals      208 0.96295 0.004630 0.60312                          
Total             225 1.59661                                           
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Call: procD.lm(f1 = shape ~ species * sex, iter = 9999, RRPP = F, data = gdf_hum,      print.progress = F)

Is that maybe already my answer? There are no different patterns of SD across the species?
Nevertheless, I would need something like pairwise comparison of the directions of shape change from male to female among all species combinations. Just coming into my mind while writting - would be 'trajectory.analysis' the right function for that?

Whether this then does correlate with the reproductive trait is a step further...I think at the moment this enough from my site.

Thank you already in advance for reading and maybe answering to my posting. I hope I was able to describe my question and problem properly and that the answers will also help other people.

Best regards,
Peter

messages.author: 511e44c7d1e1bab0
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Help with (Un)pooled regression´s and model comparisons
parts:
Peter,

I´m afraid this is a whole research project, which is difficult to address in an email thread, and possibly quite beyond the scope of a mailing list, but I´ll try to address some of your points:

- the species*sex interaction is telling you whether the degree and type of SD is the same or not across species

- the interaction of CS with a categorical variable is telling you whether allometric slopes are the same across groups or not

- to explore the full model, you would need something like shape ~ CS*species*sex to review the complete set of main effects and interactions

- throughout, you are setting RRPP = F, which is not the best of ideas, please see Collyer & Adams 2018 MEE (https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13029) and references therein for why this is the case

- for post-hoc tests see pairwise() to explore which pairs of groups might be different in different aspects

- a thorough explanation of all the above is available in the geomorph vignette called geomorph.assistance (aka Addition by Subtraction: Improving geomorph with fewer functions)

Hope this helps

Antigoni

Hello Antigoni,

thank you for your fast answer which helped me already a bit. In a first, I read no dramatic flaws from your posting in my analysis so far^^

So, I will adapt my script to your comments and explore a full model including CS, rather than eliminate the size-component by applying residuals of the allometry model to the mean shape.

I went into more detail in trajectory analysis, which I think now makes sense to apply. I developed the following code so far. If I look at the graph, which should show the direction of shape change from females to males, the 'summary'-result of the applied trajectory analysis makes sense the one, red species being significant to most of the others while from the others they all go in the same direction i.e. exhibiting similar SD explaining why species:sex interaction is only "close" to significance as the majority of species show equal pattern except the red one. Please correct me if I did misinterpret the output of that script.

rrpp.hum<-rrpp.data.frame(shape=matrix_hum,sex=sexH,CS=CS_hum,species=speciesH)
trac.sex<-lm.rrpp(shape~species*sex,data=rrpp.hum,iter=999,print.progress=F)
anova(trac.sex)

parts:
Hello everybody,

I just struggle a bit (or a bit more) with the more complex models and get confused about what I read and what is shown in the literature.

So my "full" model shape~CS*species*sex is according to the 'anova()'-function the best one explaining most of my variance if compared to "simpler" models.
The output is as following:
Df      SS       MS     Rsq       F             Z        Pr(>F)
Call: procD.lm(f1 = shape ~ CS * species * sex, iter = 9999, RRPP = T,
data = gdf_hum, print.progress = F)

So, I have different allometries between species but not sexes, and different sexual dimorphims between the species. And what ever a three-factor interaction could mean...
If I understand it correctly from what I did read also here in this group, I cannot remove any factor from that model as every factor is interacting in some kind with another one, e.g. just have a look on shape~CS+sex to have a look and visualize sex-shape differences.

Dear Antigoni, I found then your paper "Evolutionary History and Not Heterochronic Modifications Associated with Viviparity Drive Head Shape Differentiation in a Reproductive Polymorphic Species, Salamandra salamandra" which deals also with several factors and I think could be compared in methology what I want to do. Actually, I am not able to really figure out the models run for Table 1. It is stated that population is always nested within subspecies. If I ran a nested model e.g. shape~species/sex I get as a result p-values for 'species' and 'species:sex', but not for 'sex' only! But for that kind of model in Table1 'population' is listed separately as variable?! For my understanding in (c) then the interaction term of CS*subsp.*pop. is missing, if I assume a model like shape~CS*subspec./population ?!
Likely I do misunderstand or misinterpret something.

confused regards,
Peter

messages.author: 511e44c7d1e1bab0
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Re: Help with (Un)pooled regression´s and model comparisons
parts:
Peter, I´m not sure how to help here, but for the sake of the general discussion in the list, I need to notify you that the article you mentioned on Salanamders, is absolutely NOT a good example for a general understanding of interaction terms and allometry, as that system is very complex (biologically, that is) and it includes nested factors and not fully overlapping interactive ones. So definitely NOT a good read unless you first understand linear models very well.

I might recommend that you start by reading some more general literature on the subject. Maybe the practical companion to to Geometric Morphometrics for Biologists, written by Mimi Zelditch and Don Swirderski could be a good read for this. You can find it here:

https://www.researchgate.net/publication/328215969_A_Practical_Companion_to_Geometric_Morphometrics_for_Biologists_Running_analyses_in_freely-available_software_Second_Edition

Good luck!

Antigoni
